en: The Brāhmaṇa on the Establishment of the Sacred Fires (*Agnnyādheya*). The exponents of sacred knowledge say: "In ancient times, Auddālaki Āruṇi said: 'I offer thee, acceptable to Brahman and to the out-breath (*prāṇa*); I offer thee, acceptable to Brahman and to the in-breath (*apāna*); I offer thee, acceptable to Brahman and to the diffused breath (*vyāna*); I offer thee, acceptable to Brahman and to the levelled breath (*samāna*). Who are these deities to whom he offers what is acceptable? The *ṛc*-verses are indeed the out-breath of Brahman; it is to the *ṛc*s that he thus offers what is acceptable. The *yajus*-formulas are indeed the in-breath of Brahman; it is to the *yajus* that he thus offers what is acceptable."

The Sāmans are indeed the Vyāna breath of Brahman; he thus offers what is dear to the Sāmans. The Atharvans are indeed the Samāna breath of Brahman; he thus offers what is dear to the Atharvans. It consists of four spoonfuls, for there are these four Vedas; he thereby makes them partakers. The Veda is indeed the root of Brahman; that which the officiating priests consume is the root of the Vedas—this is why it is called *brahmaudana* (the food of Brahman).

At night, the Brahman priest offers the *brahmaudanā* (the rice for the Brahman). Indeed, the *rakṣases* sought to strike at the sacrifice of the gods; they drove them away by means of the *brahman*. The Brahman priest is the *brahman*; verily, by the *brahman* alone he drives the *rakṣases* away from the sacrifice. It consists of four *śarāvas* (measures); there are four quarters; verily, by the quarters he drives the *rakṣases* away from the sacrifice. It consists of whole grains, for the sake of prosperity.

He who establishes the sacred fire (*agni*) without having paid his debts is indeed impure, unholy, unfit for sacrifice, and has spoken untruth; having caused him to touch [the fire], he offers these oblations of clarified butter with the verses: "O gods, whatever offense against the gods... and "Whatever debt I incurred while not gambling... He thereby purifies him; purified, holy, and fit for sacrifice, he establishes the fire. He offers twenty-one oblations; that sun is the twenty-first, it is Savitṛ, and he is the purifier of the god Savitṛ. By means of that very purifier of Savitṛ, he purifies him. With the verse beginning "That which is the atmosphere... [he offers] to Agni.

In this way they release him from this sin; with the words "saṃkasuka, vikasuka," the fires drive away his consumption (yakṣma), magic spell (kṛtyā), and destruction (nirṛti); and with the words "saṃ varcase," he invokes a blessing. 2.

The gods and the Asuras were once gathered for the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), competing with one another. Whatever the gods did, the Asuras did the same. Those gods, having set down this rice-offering (odana), offered these oblations with clarified butter (ājya). The Asuras could not follow that; consequently, the gods prevailed and the Asuras were defeated. He who, knowing thus, sets down this rice-offering and offers these oblations with clarified butter, does so to prevent his rival from following after him; he prospers himself, and his rival is defeated. Having recited, "For Pravedhas, O sages... [he offers] of the rice.

He offers oblations; verily he expiates the offenses against the gods. For one who is about to undertake the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and is about to undergo consecration (*dīkṣā*), he offers these oblations with clarified butter. He purifies him; purified, fit for sacrifice, and worthy of the sacrifice, he performs the rite. Purified, fit for sacrifice, and worthy of the sacrifice, he undergoes consecration. On the night before he is to establish the fires, they remain awake. Sleep is indeed blind darkness; verily he releases him from that blind darkness. They sing with artistic skills (*śilpa*); for by means of artistic skills they accomplish everything. 3.

One should maintain this fire: one should not eat meat, one should not approach a woman, one should sleep on the ground, one should not go away from home, and they should not carry the fire away from his house; nor should others carry it away, for its protection. Having established this fire, he should perform the rites ending with the placing of the fuel-sticks. He releases his speech with the words, "I give a boon. For this fire, having become unappeased, approaches the sacrificer; by means of the boon and by means of true speech, he pacifies it. 4.

When the Gārhapatya fire is being established, he sings the Rathantara; the Rathantara is this world, and the Gārhapatya is this world: by means of it, he finds firm footing in this world and secures Agni as light. When the Dakṣiṇāgni fire is being established, he sings the Vāmadevya; the Vāmadevya is the intermediate space, and the Dakṣiṇāgni is the intermediate space: by means of it, he finds firm footing in the intermediate space and secures Vāyu as light. When the Āhavanīya fire is being established, he sings the Bṛhat; the Bṛhat is yonder world, and the Āhavanīya is yonder world: by means of it, he finds firm footing in yonder world.

The sun becomes firmly established; he wins the light. Regarding this, they say: "The fires of one for whom *sāmans* are sung while they are being laid down have indeed been laid down. For the *sāmans* are the calves of the fires; they do not yield all blessings for him. Therefore, the *sāmans* should not be sung for the fires, lest they fail to yield. The *sāmans* are indeed the dear bodies of Soma. If they were sung elsewhere, one would deprive Soma of his dear bodies; Soma would not be inclined toward him. Therefore, the *sāmans* should not be sung, for the sake of bringing Soma near.

One who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should not turn away a Brāhmaṇa guest in the evening, even if he has already traveled with the sun; for the sun indeed enters the Brāhmaṇa in the evening. When a guest comes to one who has established the fires, he, being satisfied, enters the fire. Therefore, he must not be turned away. No Brāhmaṇa should dwell in his house without having eaten. He would consume the progeny, the cattle, and the meritorious deeds of that man, for it is for the sake of giving that he establishes the fire. One should not eat until the fire has been offered oblations in the morning and evening after sunrise; for such a person is the guest of the one who has established the fires before [the offerings].

They honor the guest. One should not eat food cooked on a *ṛbhīsa* (a vessel made of reeds), for that is impurity (*śamala*) to Agni. One should not dwell in a natural pit (*svakṛta iriṇa*), nor should one place wet wood upon the fire, for that is not of Agni's nature. One should not sip water from river-water (*nāvyudaka*), for the fire in river-water mounts the one who maintains the sacred fires; [one should do this] for its pacification. One should not speak untruth, for untruth is impurity of speech; he would become seized by impurity. For twelve nights he should offer the *agnihotra* with clarified butter; his fires are like those newly born, just as a newborn child.

Just as one causes clarified butter to settle, even so does that fire become perpetual. Indeed, the *rakṣases* and the spirits (*bhūta*) gather together; for he who establishes the sacred fire becomes a spirit among the gods. Agni is the slayer of the *rakṣases* among the gods, for the purpose of driving away the *rakṣases*. He should wear unwashed clothing for the sake of purity and also for the sake of brilliance. He gives two garments to the *adhvaryu*, for he thus establishes him in the *virāj* (the sovereign). Regarding this, there is this verse:

"High in heaven stand those who give sacrificial fees; those who give horses dwell with the sun. Those who give gold partake in immortality; those who give clothing, O Soma, prolong their lives. At the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, she gives a garment to her husband. A pair of cattle should be given so that they may grow old together, for the attainment of a productive couple. Furthermore, he becomes a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) for the protection of himself. 5.

The Gārhapatya fire is indeed the chief among the fires; for originally there was only this one—the Āhavanīya did not exist, nor the Dakṣiṇāgni. Those gods, together with their wives, cooked food on the Gārhapatya; having cooked it, they ate it as a communal meal. But the divine wives did not eat, saying, "Let us go. The gods understood, "This is an injury to the sacrifice; let us divide the fire," and so they divided the fire. That third part of the fire which remained, the gods brought forward the next day toward the east for the sake of the gods.

It became the Āhavanīya; that is the reason for the Āhavanīya’s status as the Āhavanīya. Therefore, day after day, it is carried forward toward the east. That third part of the fire which the divine ancestors (devapitaraḥ) seized and led away to the south—that became the Dakṣiṇāgni; that is the reason for the Dakṣiṇāgni’s status as the Dakṣiṇāgni. Just as a son born from a Vṛṣalī womb eats everything, both pure and impure, even so does the Bhrāṣṭrāgni eat everything, both pure and impure; for this [fire] belongs to the Asuras.

Because the fire is in the hearth (bhrāṣṭra) and because one offers oblations into it, his oblations become non-solar (asurya); indeed, he previously cooked what was cooked for the Asuras and not for the Pitṛs. Now, if one should desire, "May my portion for the Pitṛs be uncooked," he should lead forth the fire from the Gārhapatya and offer the oblations; thus his portion for the Pitṛs becomes truly uncooked. The third part of that [fire] the wives of the gods grasped around; that became the Gārhapatya. That is the reason for the Gārhapatya's name, "Gārhapatya."

Therefore, they perform the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives at the Gārhapatya fire within an enclosed space; these have clarified butter as their oblation. Clarified butter is indeed seed, and from seed offspring are born; [thus it serves] for procreation. One should make the mark of the Gārhapatya circular, for this world is circular, and it is commensurate with this world. Half-moon-shaped is that of the Dakṣiṇāgni, for the intermediate region is half-moon-shaped, and it is commensurate with the intermediate region. The heavenly world is square; therefore, the Āhavanīya is square, for the attainment of the heavenly world.

The exponents of Brahman say: "These are indeed the abodes of the gods—the Gārhapatya, the Dakṣiṇāgni, and the Āhavanīya. One should make the mark of the Gārhapatya circular, for this world is circular; it is twenty-eight finger-breadths wide, commensurate with the Śakvarī metre. The Śakvarī consists of seven feet, and cattle are related to the Śakvarī; thus, he wins cattle."

The crescent moon is the southern fire-altar; the crescent moon is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and it is measured by the intermediate space. This moon is indeed the food of the deities; thus he causes the deities themselves to enjoy his food. It is thirty-two finger-breadths wide, commensurate with the *anuṣṭubh* meter; through the *anuṣṭubh* he produces vigor, and by means of the vigor of the *anuṣṭubh* he brings the sacrificer to fulfillment. He should make the Āhavanīya fire-altar square, for that world is square; it is one cubit long, for the self is of this size and is commensurate with Prajāpati. Prajāpati is indeed food; thus he brings him to fulfillment through the eating of food.

Having offered the oblations, he should release the fires; he is then procreated with offspring and cattle. Now they say: "For once released, the bull grows. With the words, "Spread yourself out with the measure of heaven, with width," he indeed spreads it out. Just as one who is glowing adds more fuel, even so does he place splendor into him in succession. Regarding this, they say: "Who is fit to awaken one who is sleeping better than himself? Therefore, he should not release them. He who knows their abode becomes possessed of an abode. For him who knows thus, and for him for whom one who knows thus arranges the fires, he becomes more prosperous. 7

All the gods, having come together, asked Prajāpati, "From where shall the three sacred fires arise? He performed penance for a thousand divine years, standing with his feet upwards and his head towards the ground below. Tears fell from him; from those very tears, the horse was born. It turned around, it shook itself, it voided dung, and turning back, it sniffed the ground; from that, the *śaka* (the horse-fly) and the *aśva* (horse) were born. From its sides and from its middle, the *aśvattha* tree was born; its Veda is [the sacrificial grass].
The roots are the meters, and the branches are the intermediate branches; thus is this the Śamī-womb, and that is the reason for the Śamī-womb’s name "Śamī-womb. 8.

All the gods, having come together, asked Prajāpati: "From what does this Agni arise—whether from a union, or from the lower fire-drill (araṇi), or from the upper one? To them Prajāpati replied: "Just as when a man approaches a woman, from that union, through the friction of the male, semen is produced; this indeed is the form of Viṣṇu which is the upper fire-drill, and that is the form of the Gāyatrī. Therefore, from this union, Agni is born when being churned. The upper [drill] is twelve finger-breadths long; there are twelve months."

The umbrella is thirteen finger-breadths wide for the attainment of the year; these worlds are three, and the year consists of ten months—for the attainment of the year. The handle is for the three seasonal libations; he prospers in these very worlds. 9.

Agni indeed departed from the gods; he ran away facing westward. Therefore, the Adhvaryu churns the fire while facing westward. In that he churns the fire facing westward, he calls upon that very Agni with the words, "Thy brilliant smoke rises up. In that he sings a Sāman over the smoke, he announces him to the gods. With the words, "The best finder of the way," in that he sings a Sāman over the fire, he makes him known as an announcement to the gods. This fire is indeed a child, yet it is full of brilliance. Therefore, no Sāmans are sung at the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), for [it would diminish] its brilliance.

For these fires of his do not endure it; they cry out against him whose Sāmans are sung before the Soma [pressing]. Therefore, the Sāmans should be sung during the Soma [pressing], neither before nor after the Soma, so that the fires may possess the nature of fire and also for the sake of their brilliance.

The fire-drill (araṇi) is twenty-four finger-breadths long; the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables, and it is measured by the Gāyatrī. It is six finger-breadths wide; there are six seasons, and thus he finds firm support in the seasons. Viṣṇu is indeed the lower fire-drill (ara), and this upper fire-drill (araṇi) is his wife; that is why the upper fire-drill is called *araṇī*. Of that [upper drill], the first four finger-breadths are the head; the next four finger-breadths are the neck; the next four finger-breadths are the chest, the breast, the arms, the sides, the back, and the belly; and what remains beyond those...

Four finger-breadths constitute her hips; the other four finger-breadths are her thighs; the next four finger-breadths are her knees; and the final four finger-breadths are her shanks and feet—it is by this much alone that the fire-drill is complete in all its limbs. If one churns it in the head, the sacrificer dies of a disease of the head; if in the mouth, he becomes deficient in speech; if in the neck, he becomes stammering; if in the shoulders, he becomes paralyzed on one side; and if in the belly, the sacrificer dies of hunger.

What [he churns] from the thighs belongs to the *yātudhānas*; what from the shanks belongs to the *piśācas*; what from the feet belongs to the flesh-eaters (*kravyādas*); what he churns from the hips belongs to all the gods. By means of that, the sacrificer who knows thus becomes one who goes to heaven. At the first churning, there are established rules for the positions; in the others, there are none. And he who knows thus does not fall into falsehood. 11. Thus ends the *Brāhmaṇa* on the Establishment of the Fires (*Agnnyādheya*), the *Amā-brāhmaṇa*.

The gods and the Asuras churned the essence of the waters; from that which was being churned, the nectar (amṛta) arose. From that, the essence which flowed forth on all sides became Soma; that is the reason for Soma’s name "Soma. Indeed, Soma is the Moon, and the gods consume him in the vessel. Man consists of sixteen parts: "hair" is two syllables, "skin" is two, "blood" is two, "flesh" is two, "sinew" is two, "bone" is two, "marrow" is two, and "semen" is two. These amount to sixteen; thus he is this one of sixteen parts.

Of that Soma, the Vasus consumed five portions as the Puruṣa; making the earth their vessel, they desired immortality and they attained immortality. Thereupon they became immortal, satisfied, and gratified. Of that [Soma], the Rudras consumed five portions; making the intermediate space their vessel, they desired immortality and they attained immortality. Thereupon they became immortal, satisfied, and gratified. Of that [Soma], the Ādityas consumed five portions; making the sky their vessel...

They desired immortality; they won immortality. Thereupon, having become immortal, they became satisfied and pleased. One digit remained; Prajāpati gave it to Sinīvālī. It settled here among the cattle, the trees, and the plants; because it settled (*avasat*) in the *amā* (home), that is the origin of the name *amāvāsyā*. With her [that digit], he saw [the moon] in the morning; because he saw (*dadarśa*) it, that is the origin of the name *darśa*. When the gods had arrived at the sacrifice, they caused him, who was already full, to swell again. He, being full, settled on the *paurṇamāsī* (full-moon day); that is the origin of the name *paurṇamāsī*.

"Therefore, they say that one who performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices goes forth conquering the worlds; he attains equality of power, union, and the same world as Soma—this for him who, knowing thus, sacrifices with the New and Full Moon sacrifices. This is the *Amāvāsyā Brāhmaṇa*...
[the Brāhmaṇa].
"Four are his horns"—this refers to the Vedas;
"three are his feet"—this refers to the three *savana*s;
"two are his heads"—these refer to the *prāyaṇīya* and *udayanīya* [offerings].
"Seven hands"— these are the seven meters;
therefore there are seven flames, seven fuel-sticks,
and these seven worlds in which the vital breaths move, hidden in the cave, placed seven by seven.

"Bound in three ways" means bound in a threefold manner by the Mantras, Brāhmaṇas, and Kalpas. "The Bull roars"—the roaring of this [Veda] occurs according to the sequence of the sacrifices (*savanas*): with *Ṛks*, *Yajus*, *Sāmans*, and *Atharvans*. When they praise him with *Ṛks*, sacrifice with *Yajus*, laud him with *Sāmans*, and mutter prayers with *Atharvans*. "The great god"—that is, Mahādeva—"has entered mortals," that is, human beings. For his further explanation, there are more [verses] to follow. "Four horns"—there were four faces, four Vedas, four ages, and four fires.

Itself, it becomes one named Mount Kailāsa; it becomes one peak, two peaks, ten peaks, twelve peaks, twenty peaks, twenty-two peaks, thirty peaks, thirty-two peaks, a hundred peaks, a thousand peaks, ten million peaks, infinite peaks, the peak of Meru, the peak of crystal, the peak of the ancestors, and the peak of humanity. The sages declare that it is the beginning and end of the twelve Ādityas; he who knows this attains all life, attains the full span of life, attains everything—this is the *Graheṣṭibrāhmaṇa*.

The gods and the asuras performed the sacrifice equally; whatever the gods did, the asuras did that too. Those gods saw these oblations of the cups (graha-havīṃṣi) and with them they caused Indra to sacrifice; the asuras did not follow after them. Thereupon the gods prevailed and the asuras were defeated. He who, knowing thus, performs these oblations of the cups does so for the sake of his rival’s non-following; he prevails himself and his rival is defeated. He should offer a pap of cooked rice in ghee to Āditya; thereby [he gains] brilliance.

He purchases with it the splendor of the Śukra [star] by means of an oblation of rice-porridge (*caru*) in milk; he purchases with it the power of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*) belonging to Bṛhaspati by means of an oblation of wild rice (*naivāra*) in milk; he purchases with it the lordship of speech (*vākpatya*) by means of an oblation on eleven potsherds for Bodha; he purchases with it intelligence (*buddhi*) by means of an oblation on one potsherd for Bhūma; he purchases with it glory (*yaśas*) by means of an oblation of meat mixed with ghee in ghee for Saura; he purchases with it long life (*āyus*) by means of an oblation on fifteen potsherds for Candra; he purchases with it freedom from fear (*abhaya*) by means of an oblation of rice-porridge for Rāhu.

He purchases these very [offering materials] by means of that [sacrificial fee], which prevents their exclusion; thus, for one who, knowing this, should sacrifice with this [rite], all these things indeed come to be. He offers the secondary oblations (*upahoma*) with clarified butter for the attainment of blessings. One who desires: "May I be radiant, brilliant, a lord of speech, wise, glorious, fragrant, long-lived, and one whose cattle are never excluded," should sacrifice with this [rite]. There are eighteen *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses beginning with "The single wheel rising, shining... for the sake of uniformity; [the deities are] Agni, Hiraṇya, Soma...

"Hiraṇyam" and "preddho agne imo agne" are the two *ājyabhāga* offerings; he sacrifices loudly with these as the *saṃyājyās*. This is indeed the highest of all forms of speech; by sacrificing loudly, he becomes the highest among his equals and radiant like the sun. He offers the *upahoma* oblations for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. Whoever, knowing this, should sacrifice with this [rite]—this is the *upanayana-brāhmaṇa*.

"I have come for the holy life (*brahmacarya*)," he says. For "Brahman" is indeed the Brahmin; by means of the Brahman, he thus entrusts himself. He asks him, "What is your name? For "Ka" is indeed Prajāpati; having thus made him one who belongs to Prajāpati and possessing a kinship, he initiates him. He says, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. By this, he bestows these three worlds upon him for the sake of food. "Bhūḥ" is indeed this world, "bhuvaḥ" is the intermediate space, and "svaḥ" is yonder world; by this, he bestows these three Vedas upon him for the sake of food. "Bhūḥ" is indeed the *ṛc*s...

"Bhuvaḥ" refers to the Yajus formulas; "Svaḥ" refers to the Sāmans. He who knows this studies one, two, three, or all of these Vedas. To whomsoever he, knowing this, initiates, he says: "To Ka I entrust you. Ka, indeed, is Prajāpati; thus he entrusts him to Prajāpati. His student does not die, nor does his student perish, for whomsoever he, knowing this, initiates. To him he says: "To the god Savitṛ I entrust you. For it is Savitṛ who impels whatever here is produced for living beings.

Whatever they do, he should not think, "I am doing this," if he himself were to do it; rather, he should think, "The Sun (Savitṛ) has caused this for me. Indeed, whatever is auspicious, that the Sun brings forth for him; the Sun does not bring forth evil for him. To whomsoever he, knowing this, initiates, he says: "I entrust you to Bṛhaspati. Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; thus he entrusts him to the Brahman. His student does not die, nor does his student perish, for him who knows this.

The learned man initiates him and says to him, "Thou art a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*). Verily, sacred knowledge is food; thus he places food within him. Moreover, sacred knowledge is immortality; thus he places immortality within him. He says to him, "Eat water. Verily, the waters pervaded this entire universe; thus he says to him, "Pervade all. Verily, the waters are food; thus he places food within him. Moreover, the waters are immortality; thus he places immortality within him. He says to him, "Perform thy work. Verily, work is vigor; by vigor, indeed, food is eaten.

[The breath] is either action or food; he thus bestows food upon him. Moreover, [the breath] is either immortality or food; he thus bestows immortality upon him. He says to him, "Do not sleep by day. Sleep is indeed death; therefore, he drives it away. For sleep is indeed death; therefore, when someone dies, they say of him, "He has slept a long sleep. By day, indeed, is food; he thus bestows food upon him. Moreover, food is indeed immortality; he thus bestows immortality upon him. He says to him, "Restrain your speech. Speech, indeed, is...

He places food upon him; verily, he bestows food upon him. Moreover, immortality is indeed food; he thus bestows immortality upon him. These are the five kinds of food that the teacher places before the recitation of the Sāvitrī for the religious student.

This very student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) is born together with the Sāvitrī. Regarding this they say: "It should be recited after a year; for seeds, once sown, are born after a year. But they also say: "It should be recited after twelve days; for twelve months make a year; thus he causes him to be born by means of the year, for the attainment of the year. One should recite that [Sāvitrī] at dawn after three nights. There are three days, three nights, three twilights, and three dawns; these amount to twelve. Twelve months [make a year].

The year [is the sacrifice]; verily, by means of the year he causes him to be born for the attainment of the year. This [verse] is indeed the Sāvitrī; it is the stepping-stone for these worlds and for these Vedas. One should not recite it while standing, nor while squatting, nor while walking. Having spread out his lap and sitting facing east, he recites it for one sitting facing west. Prajāpati faces east, and the gods are dependent upon him from the west. The teacher is Prajāpati; thus, by means of the deity, he establishes the student in his proper abode. Now, one...

They say that one recites for her while sitting to the south. If he were to recite for her while standing sideways, the embryo would enter him sideways and would injure him; therefore, sitting facing east, he recites for her as she sits facing west. For the breath moves forward; thus he places breath within him. He should recite it three times; there are three breaths—out-breath (*prāṇa*), diffused breath (*vyāna*), and in-breath (*apāna*)—and these he places within him. Or he may recite it twice, for there are two breaths, out-breath and in-breath; thus he places the out-breath and in-breath within him.
Or he may recite it once at the end, combining them all, for there is but one breath; thus he places breath within him. This is the *Śrāddhabrāhmaṇa*.

These worlds belonged to the Asuras. The gods said, "Whosoever among us shall conquer a world, that world shall belong to him. The Vasus conquered this world; the Rudras, the intermediate space; and the Ādityas, the sky. Having conquered this world, the Vasus flew away toward the intermediate space. Those Rudras said, "What we have won, let that be ours together with you. Then the Vasus and the Rudras, having conquered the intermediate space, flew away toward the sky. They said to the Ādityas, "What we have won, let that be ours together with you. Thus they [the Ādityas] spoke.

The Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas conquered that world, and by doing so, they overcame the Asuras in these very worlds. Then the gods prevailed, and the Asuras were defeated. The Vasus became the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and the Ādityas the great-grandfathers. Therefore, people say, "The gods are the fathers," and "The fathers are the gods. Those among the gods who are Soma-drinkers are the fathers; one satisfies them with vessels of water. Therefore, three times as much water is given for one [deceased], twice for another, and once for another; thus it amounts to six, and they obtain exactly what was won.

The water which they drink from the vessel is the seventh; that which is mixed with sesame seeds from both sides is the eighth; the sprinkling of water around the rice-balls from the dish is the ninth; and when they pour out the water-pitcher as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), that is the tenth. Therefore, this Śrāddha is called "the ten-fold water-rite" (daśodaka). That consists of ten parts, and the Virāj meter has ten syllables; the Virāj is food. Thus, he becomes established in the Virāj, in the enjoyment of food. 1.

The ancestors indeed followed their son as he was being born, thinking, "May he perform the *śrāddha* for us. He said, "When shall I perform the *śrāddha*? They replied, "One who desires that it should not be given again should give the *śrāddha* in the shadow of an elephant. Svarbhānu, having become an elephant, overwhelmed yonder sun with his shadow. The divine ancestors (devapitṛs) then nourished him; therefore, the shadow of an elephant is the abode of the divine ancestors. For this reason, one should give the *śrāddha* in the shadow of an elephant.

One should desire that it be inexhaustible, immeasurable, infinite, and abundant; for one who, knowing this, gives a *śrāddha* in the shadow of an elephant, it becomes truly inexhaustible, immeasurable, infinite, and abundant for the sake of the ancestors' inexhaustibility.

There are indeed two paths: the path of the gods (*devayāna*) and the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāna*). By means of the *agnihotra*, the gods went to the heavenly world; by means of the sacrifice to the fathers (*pitṛyajña*), they went to the world of the fathers. Therefore, both should be sacrificed to—the path of the gods and the path of the fathers—for it is said that by both of these one goes to the heavenly world. In another world, they established themselves with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and they withdrew food from the Brahmins. They said to them: "We shall act in the fire! We will act in the fire! Let us act in the fire! They replied: "Act! Act! Let it be done! To him—

If he should desire, "May he be possessed of offspring," one should say to him, "Perform it at his sacrifice. If he should desire, "May he be possessed of cattle," one should say to him, "Perform it for him at the sacrifice. If he should desire, "May he become more prosperous," one should say to him, "Let it be performed at his sacrifice. For this oblation offered in the fire is indeed dedicated to Agni and Soma; by means of this oblation dedicated to Agni and Soma, the sacrificer becomes more prosperous in this world. 3.

He who prepares himself for sacrifice yokes his mind; for it is with the mind that the sacrifice is performed, and thus he becomes a sacrificer. Then he places his faith, for the ancestors follow after one who has faith. When they perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* upon hearing of prosperity, by that means their beloved ones become pleased with him. Indra, desiring offspring, sacrificed with the Pitṛyajña. The Asuras sought to destroy his sacrifice, but the Viśvedevas struck them down. Therefore, they perform the Vaiśvadeva offering first, for the purpose of driving away the Asuras.

It should be given on ground sloping toward the east; for the thunderbolt is indeed inclined toward the east, and by means of the thunderbolt he drives away the Rakṣases from the sacrifice. The Darbha grass-blades have their tips pointing southward and northward; for with those whose tips point southward his ancestors approach him, and with those whose tips point northward the gods approach. Therefore, the Darbha grass is handed over to the Brāhmaṇas turned back [toward the south], so that it may reach the ancestors. In this way his ancestors approach him, for the ancestors are hidden from yonder sun, and likewise they are hidden from the gods.

From among humans, the Pitṛs receive the base of the *barhis* grass, and by that [base] the Pitṛs are honored; that which is without a base belongs to the Devas. Thus both are worshipped, for they are hidden from the sight of a human; for in this very way they remain hidden.
4. This is the Śrāddha-Brāhmaṇa, the Mekhalā-Brāhmaṇa.

"This one, warding off ill-spoken words"—thus, having avoided ill-spoken words, they ward [evil] away. "She has come to us, purifying the color and the filter"—the waters indeed are the color; she makes the filter pure. "Bringing strength through out-breath and in-breath"—she bestows strength through the out-breath and in-breath. "This auspicious, blessed goddess, the girdle"—verily, he invokes this blessing; the auspicious goddess bestows good fortune. "May they extend our life by a thousandfold"—this is the Brāhmaṇa on the girdle.
